Fever up to 39 °C for 4 days, cough, weakness, rapid breathing.
Doctor, my son has had a fever for four days, up to 39. His cough got worse, he is not eating, and since last night his breathing has become fast.
Four days ago he had a runny nose and sneezed. On the second day the fever rose to 38.5, then it stayed at 39 and would not come down.
Yes, 39–39.5. When I give paracetamol it comes down for an hour or two, then rises again. It has gone on for more than three days.
At first a dry cough, from the second day it became wet. Since last night he has been breathing faster, and the spaces between his ribs pull in when he breathes.
Only paracetamol and nose drops. We did not give antibiotics.
All vaccinations are on schedule, including those against pneumococcal and Haemophilus infections.
Many children in his kindergarten group have had colds.
No one in the family has had tuberculosis or a long-lasting cough.
He catches colds 2–3 times a year, has never had pneumonia.
No allergy to medicines or food has been noticed.
He vomited once while coughing, stool is normal.
For the third day he has barely eaten, drinking water in small sips.
Condition moderately severe, signs of intoxication present: weak, fussy, no appetite.
Skin pale, mild cyanosis of the nasolabial triangle, worse when restless.
Nasal flaring on breathing. Throat mucosa hyperemic.
Dyspnea of mixed type (RR 46/min). Retraction of the intercostal and substernal areas. Vocal fremitus increased below the scapula on the right.
Abdomen soft, painless. Liver 1.5 cm below the costal margin (appropriate for age). Spleen not palpable.
Meningeal signs negative (no nuchal rigidity, Kernig negative).
**White blood cells 16.8×10⁹/L**, **neutrophils 78% (band 9%)**, lymphocytes 18%, Hb 118 g/L, **ESR 32 mm/h**.
**CRP 64 mg/L** (normal < 5).
**Inhomogeneous infiltrative shadow in the right lower lobe.** No fluid in the pleural cavity. Heart shadow unchanged.
Specific gravity 1.024, traces of protein, white blood cells 2–3 (in the setting of fever).
Cannot be performed because of the patient's age (after 5 years).

Acute obstructive bronchitis
Acute simple bronchitis

Exudative pleurisy

Persistent high fever for more than 3 days, intoxication, tachypnea (≥ 40/min at 3 years — WHO criterion), intercostal retraction and nasal flaring point to pneumonia. Dullness of the percussion note below the right scapula, increased vocal fremitus and crepitations on a background of diminished breathing are the physical signs of an infiltration focus. On X-ray, infiltration in the right lower lobe, leukocytosis with a left shift and raised CRP confirm a bacterial process. SpO₂ 93% and dyspnea — respiratory failure grade I.
In bronchitis the percussion note is unchanged and rales are scattered; in pneumonia the findings are focal and asymmetric.
In children up to 5–6 years puerile breathing is normal (expiration is also heard well).
Tachypnea thresholds (WHO): under 2 months ≥ 60, 2–12 months ≥ 50, 1–5 years ≥ 40 breaths/min.
Vocal fremitus is increased in infiltration and decreased when there is fluid in the pleural cavity.

Cardiovascular
Tires easily, short of breath when running, often has bronchitis.

My daughter can't run like other children, she gets tired quickly and short of breath. She has bronchitis several times a year. She also gains little weight. The kindergarten nurse told me to have her heart checked.
After running a little she gets short of breath, has to stop, and sweats. Her lips don't turn blue, she doesn't squat down to rest.
She has been hospitalized with bronchitis 4–5 times a year and with pneumonia twice.
In the 2nd month of pregnancy I had a bad cold with fever and took medicine. She was born at term, 3100 g.
Walking and talking on time. But her weight gain was always poor, and as a baby she tired quickly and sweated when nursing.
No congenital heart defect in the family. Her grandmother has hypertension.
From infancy she sweated while feeding. After age three, tiredness and shortness of breath became noticeable.
Mainly tiredness, shortness of breath and frequent bronchitis. No chest pain or fainting.
No cough now. She coughs during bronchitis.
Vaccinations complete.
Condition satisfactory. Physical development slightly behind age (weight deficit ~ 10%).
Skin pale, no cyanosis. Fingers unchanged (no “drumstick” clubbing).
Slight bulge in the cardiac area (cardiac hump). Both sides take part equally in breathing.

Apex beat strengthened, diffuse, in the 5th intercostal space 1.5 cm lateral to the midclavicular line. Systolic thrill (“cat purr”) in the 3rd–4th intercostal space at the left sternal border. Relative dullness border shifted to the left.
Abdomen soft, liver 1 cm below the costal margin.
No edema. Peripheral pulses good at all points.

**6 mm defect in the perimembranous part of the ventricular septum, left-to-right shunt.** **Left atrium and left ventricle dilated.** Systolic pressure in the pulmonary artery 38 mm Hg (mildly raised). EF 70%.
Sinus rhythm, HR 112. **Tall R wave in V5–V6 — signs of left ventricular hypertrophy.** Electrical axis normal.
**Pulmonary vascular markings increased (arterial pattern).** **Heart shadow enlarged due to the left ventricle, CTR 0.58.**
Hb 122 g/L, white blood cells 6.9×10⁹/L, ESR 7 mm/h — unchanged.
Cannot be reliably performed because of the patient's age.
Congenital heart defect: ventricular septal defect (VSD), perimembranous, circulatory failure grade I
Atrial septal defect (ASD)
Patent ductus arteriosus
Functional (innocent) systolic murmur
Tetralogy of Fallot
Rheumatic mitral regurgitation

Sweating and tiredness while feeding since infancy, poor weight gain, frequent bronchitis and pneumonias — characteristic of a pale (acyanotic) defect with pulmonary overcirculation. A harsh holosystolic murmur and systolic thrill in the 3rd–4th intercostal space at the left sternal border are the classic sign of VSD. Accentuated S2 over the pulmonary artery points to the onset of pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography confirms a perimembranous VSD.
VSD: the murmur is harsh, holosystolic, loudest at the Erb's point, with a thrill. ASD: soft murmur in the 2nd intercostal space on the left + fixed splitting of S2.
Patent ductus arteriosus: continuous “machinery” murmur below the left clavicle.
Functional murmur: soft, short, no thrill, changes with body position, does not radiate.
In tetralogy of Fallot, a “blue” defect: cyanosis, spells, squatting.

Skeletal system
Restless, sweats a lot, bald patch on the back of the head, no teeth yet, started sitting late.

My son is very restless, doesn't sleep well at night, his head gets wet with sweat when he sleeps and when he feeds. The hair on the back of his head has fallen out. He is ten months old, still has not a single tooth, and only recently began to sit.
No, we did not give vitamin D. The nurse told us to, but we forgot.
From two months old I had little milk, so we switched to cow's milk. We started complementary food at 8 months, mostly semolina porridge.
Born in November, we hardly went outside in winter. Our home is on the ground floor, little sun comes in.
He held his head up at 3 months. Began sitting at 9 months, doesn't crawl yet. No teeth.
I had anemia during pregnancy and did not take iron regularly. Born at term.
Sweating and restlessness began at 3–4 months, then the back of the head became bald.
Sweating, restlessness, absence of teeth and developmental delay.
Tends toward constipation.
No bone diseases in the family.
Vaccinations on schedule.
Condition moderately severe. Restless, easily excited, fearful.
Skin pale, moist; red dermographism. Bald patch on the back of the head.
Anterior fontanelle 3×3 cm, edges soft, pliable. Frontal and parietal bossing (“Olympian forehead”), flattened occiput. No teeth.
Thickenings at the costochondral junctions — “rachitic rosary”. Harrison's groove is present.
Abdomen enlarged, flattened (“frog belly”), muscular hypotonia, diastasis recti. Liver +2.5 cm, spleen edge can be palpated.
Thickenings at the wrists — “rachitic bracelets”. Muscular hypotonia is marked, joints lax.
Restlessness, sweating, irritability. Psychomotor development 1–2 months behind.
**Ca 2.05 mmol/L (low)**, **P 0.95 mmol/L (markedly low)**, **alkaline phosphatase 980 U/L (markedly raised)**.
**Metaphyses widened, cup-shaped, borders blurred with a “brush-like” fraying.** **Generalized osteoporosis.** Ossification centers delayed.
**Hb 104 g/L** (mild anemia), white blood cells 8.1×10⁹/L, ESR 5 mm/h.
Sulkovich test: **negative (−)** — urinary calcium excretion is reduced. Other values normal.
Cannot be performed because of the patient's age.
Rickets grade II (moderate), florid stage, subacute course
Rickets grade I (mild), initial stage
Rickets grade III (severe)
Vitamin D-resistant (hypophosphatemic) rickets
Congenital hypothyroidism
Achondroplasia

A child who did not receive vitamin D prophylaxis, was fed artificially (unadapted cow's milk) and was born in the autumn–winter season with little sun exposure — the classic risk factors of rickets. Changes in the nervous system (sweating, restlessness), bones (softening of the skull — craniotabes, bossing, rosary, bracelets, Harrison's groove) and muscles (hypotonia, “frog belly”), plus liver and spleen enlargement, are typical of grade II. Hypophosphatemia, a marked rise in alkaline phosphatase and metaphyseal changes on X-ray confirm the florid stage.
Grade I: mainly nervous and autonomic changes, minimal bone changes. Grade II: moderate changes in bones, muscles and internal organs. Grade III: severe deformities, impaired static functions.
In the initial stage Ca is normal, P slightly lowered; in the florid stage P falls sharply and alkaline phosphatase rises.
Rickets prophylaxis: vitamin D from the 1st month of life, breast milk, walks.
Ordinary doses of vitamin D do not help in hypophosphatemic rickets; family history is important.

Blood system
Pale, tires easily, no appetite, eats chalk and soil.
My daughter has become very pale. She tires quickly, plays little, doesn't eat. The strangest thing is that she wants to eat chalk from the wall and soil. She also catches colds often.
She mostly drinks cow's milk, more than a liter a day. She doesn't eat meat or liver. She drinks a lot of tea, even at mealtimes.
Pallor, weakness, no appetite. Wants to eat chalk, soil, ice. Hair is brittle, nails break.
Hemoglobin had dropped to 90 during pregnancy. Born at term.
Stool is normal, I haven't seen blood or black color in the stool.
No thalassemia or other blood diseases in the family. No jaundice.
She has been getting gradually paler for about 6 months.
ARVI 5–6 times a year.
Development appropriate for age, slowed slightly in recent months.
Conditions are good, we go out for walks.
I haven't noticed any change.
Condition moderately severe. Weak, little movement.
Skin and visible mucous membranes pale, skin dry. Fissures at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis). Nails brittle, thin. Hair dull, brittle. No jaundice.
Tongue papillae atrophied, smooth (“lacquered tongue”). Sclerae not yellow.
Lymph nodes not enlarged.
Apex beat in the age-appropriate location. Tachycardia.
Abdomen soft. Liver 1 cm below the costal margin (normal), spleen not palpable.
No edema. Muscle tone slightly decreased.

**Hb 86 g/L**, red blood cells 3.6×10¹²/L, **color index 0.7**, **MCV 64 fL**, **MCH 20 pg**, **hypochromia, microcytosis, anisocytosis**, reticulocytes 0.8%, white blood cells 7.1×10⁹/L, platelets 410×10⁹/L.
**Serum iron 5.2 µmol/L**, **ferritin 6 ng/mL**, **TIBC 84 µmol/L (raised)**, **transferrin saturation 8%**.
Occult blood (Gregersen) negative. No worm eggs found.
Bilirubin 9 µmol/L (normal), ALT 16 U/L, total protein 64 g/L.
Sinus tachycardia, HR 130. No other changes.
Iron deficiency anemia, moderate (alimentary)
Iron deficiency anemia, mild
Beta thalassemia (minor)
Hemolytic anemia
Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia
Aplastic anemia

A sideropenic syndrome (dry skin, angular cheilitis, brittle nails and hair, pica — eating chalk and soil, lacquered tongue) and an anemic syndrome (pallor, tachycardia, functional systolic murmur) occur together. The cause is alimentary: drinking a lot of cow's milk and a meat-free diet, and tea reduces iron absorption; the mother had anemia of pregnancy. Hypochromic microcytic anemia, a sharp fall in ferritin and a rise in TIBC confirm the diagnosis. Hb 86 g/L — moderate degree (70–90 g/L).
Degrees (by Hb): mild 90–110, moderate 70–90, severe < 70 g/L.
Thalassemia also has microcytosis, but ferritin is normal or raised, target cells are seen, and family history is important.
In hemolytic anemia: jaundice, splenomegaly, reticulocytosis, raised indirect bilirubin.
A soft systolic murmur in anemia is functional, related to reduced blood viscosity and faster flow.

Urinary system
Swelling of the face and eyelids in the morning, reddish-brown urine, headache.
For three days my son's eyes have been puffy in the morning. Today his urine came out reddish, like meat washings. He urinates little and says his head hurts.
About two and a half weeks ago he had a very sore throat, tonsillitis. Three days ago his eyelids swelled.
Tonsillitis two and a half weeks ago. We gave an antibiotic for 3 days and stopped when he seemed to have recovered.
Urine is reddish-brown, like meat washings. He urinates little, 3–4 times a day.
The facial swelling is worse in the morning; by evening his legs swell. Headache, weakness.
For the tonsillitis we gave amoxicillin for 3 days. Nothing now.
No kidney disease or deafness in the family.
No fever now, about 37.
No allergies.
Some classmates have had tonsillitis.
Slightly nauseated, no vomiting.
Condition moderately severe. Weak, complains of headache.
Skin pale. Edema is soft, warm, whitish. No rash or hemorrhages.
Edema of the face and eyelids ("nephritic face"), worse in the morning. Throat: tonsils slightly enlarged, no hyperemia.
Apex beat slightly strengthened. BP 135/90 mm Hg (high for age).
Abdomen soft. Pasternatsky's sign weakly positive on both sides.
Pastosity in the shin area, pitting remains on pressure.
Submandibular lymph nodes slightly enlarged, painless.
Color **"meat washings"**, specific gravity 1.028, **protein 1.2 g/L**, **red blood cells cover the whole field of view (altered)**, **casts: hyaline 3–4, red cell 1–2**, white blood cells 3–4.
**ASO 820 IU/mL (raised)**, **complement C3 0.42 g/L (low)**.
**Urea 8.9 mmol/L**, creatinine 78 µmol/L (upper limit), total protein 62 g/L, cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L.
Hb 112 g/L, white blood cells 10.2×10⁹/L, **ESR 28 mm/h**.
Kidneys slightly enlarged, **parenchymal echogenicity increased**, pelvicalyceal system not dilated.
Sinus rhythm, HR 92. No signs of left ventricular overload.
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, nephritic syndrome, renal function preserved
Nephrotic syndrome (minimal change)
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)
Acute pyelonephritis
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Urolithiasis

Edema, macrohematuria ("meat washings"), arterial hypertension and oliguria that began 2–3 weeks after streptococcal tonsillitis (latent period) are the classic picture of nephritic syndrome. A raised ASO and a low complement C3 confirm the post-streptococcal nature. Proteinuria of 1.2 g/L is below the nephrotic range, and there is no hypoproteinemia. Creatinine is at the upper limit of normal — function is preserved.
Nephritic syndrome: hematuria + hypertension + edema (+ oliguria). Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (> 50 mg/kg/day), hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, large edemas.
In IgA nephropathy hematuria appears 1–2 days after the infection (at the same time as the pharyngitis), and C3 is normal.
Normal BP in children (after age 1): systolic 90 + 2n, diastolic 60 + n (n = age in years).
In hypertension an accentuated S2 is heard over the aorta.

77 cm
Digestive system
Watery diarrhea, vomiting, fever and reduced urination for 2 days.
For two days my daughter has had watery diarrhea, 10–12 times a day. She is also vomiting and has a fever. Since this morning she has hardly urinated, and she cries without tears.
Stool is watery, yellow, in large amounts, no mucus or blood, strong smell. 10–12 times a day. Vomiting 5–6 times; she brings up even what she drinks.
In the last 8 hours she has urinated only once, very little. Her diaper is almost dry.
It began two days ago with fever and vomiting, then diarrhea followed.
Three days ago her 4-year-old brother also had diarrhea, and there are children like that in her kindergarten too.
A week ago at the polyclinic she weighed 10 kg.
Breast milk and the general family table. Now she drinks water greedily but throws it up.
We gave nothing at home, only water.
Vaccinated according to the schedule, has not received the rotavirus vaccine.
Condition severe. Restless, irritable, crying, thirsty, drinks water greedily.
Skin dry, pale. Skin pinch goes back slowly (~2 seconds). Capillary refill time 2–3 seconds. Extremities warm.
Eyes sunken, cries without tears. Anterior fontanelle almost closed, slightly sunken. Lips and oral mucosa dry.
Abdomen slightly distended, soft, diffusely painless. Bowel sounds increased. No signs of intussusception (colicky pain, "raspberry jelly" stool, abdominal mass).
Meningeal signs negative. No convulsions.
Tachycardia, pulse volume slightly decreased.
Na 136 mmol/L (isotonic), **K 3.2 mmol/L (low)**; acid–base status: **pH 7.29**, **BE −8 mmol/L** — **metabolic acidosis**.
Coprogram: white blood cells 2–3, no red blood cells, abundant neutral fat. **Rapid test for rotavirus antigen positive.**
**Hematocrit 44%** (hemoconcentration), Hb 132 g/L, white blood cells 9.8×10⁹/L, lymphocytosis.
**Specific gravity 1.030**, **acetone ++**, traces of protein.
Urea 7.2 mmol/L (slightly raised), creatinine 48 µmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L.
Acute rotavirus gastroenteritis, dehydration grade II (isotonic)
Acute gastroenteritis, dehydration grade I
Acute gastroenteritis, dehydration grade III, hypovolemic shock
Acute shigellosis (colitis syndrome)
Intestinal intussusception
Lactase deficiency

Abundant watery stool without blood that joined fever and vomiting, a family cluster and a positive rotavirus test point to viral gastroenteritis. Weight loss (10 → 9.2 kg) = 8% — dehydration grade II (6–9%). The clinical signs agree: restlessness, thirst, sunken eyes and fontanelle, no tears, slow return of the skin pinch, oliguria. Na is normal — isotonic type. Metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia are present.
Dehydration grades: I — < 5%, II — 6–9%, III — ≥ 10% loss of body weight.
In grade III: lethargy or loss of consciousness, unable to drink, skin pinch returns very slowly (> 2 s), CRT > 3 s, cold extremities, hypotension.
In shigellosis the stool is scant, with mucus and blood, and there is tenesmus (colitis syndrome).
In intussusception there is paroxysmal pain, "raspberry jelly" stool and a sausage-shaped mass in the abdomen.
7 years
122 cm
Choking attack that began at night, dry cough, difficulty breathing out.
Last night after we came back from a visit, my son woke up choking. He can't breathe out, and a whistling sound comes from his chest. He has a dry cough and can only breathe sitting up.
Yesterday at the visit he played with a cat. The choking began around 2 a.m.
As an infant he had atopic dermatitis. When he plays with a cat his eyes itch and he sneezes.
His mother (me) has allergic rhinitis, and his father had asthma as a child.
4–5 times a year they said "obstructive bronchitis"; each time inhalation helped.
We have no inhaler at home. Once we gave an aminophylline tablet.
Dry, paroxysmal cough, almost no sputum. Exhalation is difficult, with a whistling sound.
He often starts coughing when he runs, also in cold air.
No fever.
There are a lot of carpets and dust at home. We have no pets ourselves.
Condition moderately severe. Forced position: sitting, leaning on the bed with his hands (orthopnea). Speaks in broken phrases.
Skin pale, mild cyanosis of the lips and nasolabial triangle.
Nasal mucosa pale, swollen, with mucous discharge. Bluish circles under the eyes.
Chest barrel-shaped, widened. Expiratory dyspnea, accessory muscles take part in breathing, intercostal retraction. Vocal fremitus slightly diminished on both sides.
Tachycardia. Cardiac borders are hard to determine (because of lung hyperinflation).
Abdomen soft, liver at the costal margin (palpable because the diaphragm is pushed down).
**PEF 58% of predicted.** **15 minutes after salbutamol inhalation PEF +22% — bronchial obstruction is reversible.**
**Total IgE 640 kU/L (raised).** Specific IgE to cat epithelium positive.
White blood cells 8.4×10⁹/L, **eosinophils 9%**, ESR 6 mm/h.
**Lung fields hyperlucent, diaphragm domes low and flattened.** No infiltrative shadows.
CRP 4 mg/L (normal).
Bronchial asthma, atopic form, exacerbation (moderate attack)
Foreign body aspiration
Cystic fibrosis
Community-acquired pneumonia
Acute stenosing laryngotracheitis (croup)

An attack of expiratory dyspnea with orthopnea and dry cough that began at night after contact with an allergen (a cat). A history of atopy (atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis), hereditary predisposition and recurrent "obstructive bronchitis" point to bronchial asthma. Physical findings: barrel-shaped chest, a hyperresonant (boxy) note over the whole lung, diffuse dry wheezes with prolonged expiration. PEF 58% and a rise of > 12% after a bronchodilator — reversible obstruction. Eosinophilia and high IgE confirm the atopic form. SpO₂ 93% and speaking in broken phrases — a moderate attack.
In asthma the wheezes are diffuse and symmetric; in pneumonia they are focal and moist.
With a foreign body, sudden onset, unilateral diminished breathing and wheezing are typical.
A hyperresonant (boxy) note is a sign of increased lung aeration (emphysema, asthma attack).
Bronchodilator test: an increase in PEF or FEV1 of ≥ 12% shows that the obstruction is reversible.

  • BP (under 1 year): systolic 76 + 2n (n = months). After 1 year: systolic 90 + 2n, diastolic 60 + n (n = years).
  • Tachypnea (WHO): under 2 months ≥ 60, 2–12 months ≥ 50, 1–5 years ≥ 40 /min.
  • Weight (2–11 years): 10.5 + 2n kg. Height: ~100 cm at 4 years, then +6 cm each year.
  • Puerile breathing is normal from 6 months to 5–6 years. The anterior fontanelle closes at 12–18 months.
  • Neonatal jaundice (Kramer): 1 — face and neck, 2 — down to the navel, 3 — down to the knees, 4 — forearms and shins, 5 — palms and soles.
